newsitem.title: PERU: Fear of new mudslides hampers Peru disaster work.
newsitem.headline: Fear of new mudslides hampers Peru disaster work.

text.p: The fear of further mudslides hampered the search on Thursday for the bodies of 250 to 300 Peruvian peasants buried after an Andean mountainside collapsed and swept away two villages.

Distraught families sought desperately to identify the largely unrecognizable corpses being dug up, as the few survivors told harrowing stories of the torrent of mud and rocks that crashed down on them before dawn on Tuesday.
Authorities believed many bodies would remain entombed in the mud, up to 30 foot-deep (10 metre), despite the frantic work of rescuers using picks, shovels and their bare hands.
"It is most likely that many bodies are not going to be retrieved," Civil Defence official and local Mayor Luis Barra Pacheco told Reuters.
The mudslide buried the villages of Ccocha and Pumaranra in a remote mountainous region of southeastern Peru.
With clouds covering the zone at dawn on Thursday, Civil Defence workers feared it would rain later, increasing the risk of more mud slamming into scores of rescuers at the base of the slide.
At the disaster site on Wednesday, President Alberto Fujimori urged caution because of the likelihood of more mudslides.
The Civil Defence said it was flying eight sniffer dogs to the site to help locate bodies closest to the mud's surface.
Fujimori said 41 bodies had been recovered by late Wednesday, although an official at the local headquarters of the rescue operation put that figure at 47.
From a helicopter, the landslide looked like a wide brown gash on the face of the green mountainside. Rooftops poked through the mud.

"This is a disaster with very serious consequences. It has literally buried two communities where there were approximately 100 families," Fujimori said. "We calculate that there are between 250 and 300 people buried under this immense amount of mud that we are seeing here."

In the central square of nearby Kerapata, civil defence officials and forensic experts recorded details of the bodies brought in before sending them to a makeshift morgue in a schoolhouse in the neighbouring town of Tamburco.
Tears streamed down the cheeks of Lucio Huaylla Velasquez as the magnitude of the disaster began to sink in. He lost his wife, 7-year-old daughter and 18-month-old son.

"First the terrorists kill us with guns and now this," he sobbed, referring to the guerrilla wars that have plagued Peru for the past 17 years. "I have nothing, not even a box to bury them in. There is no justice."

Dressed in mourning black, Dina Rivas Tapia stared up the hill from Kerapata's town square to the landslide, handkerchief in hand. "My entire family has disappeared. They were 25 people. I have no house, no money, I don't even have a bed."
The survivors spent Wednesday night sleeping under improvised canvas shelters and in government buildings in nearby villages.

When 14-year-old Alejandra Huallya Quispe heard a loud rumbling, she grabbed her sister and leapt out of the house. "I jumped with my sister but the "huayco" (as mudslides are known locally) came and crushed my mother and other sister," she said.
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer warned of an epidemic of diseases among the 250 to 600 families left homeless by the mudslide.

The heavy rains that caused the mudslide also swelled Amazon jungle rivers in the northern province of San Martin, where floodwaters destroyed the homes of 500 families and swept away a woman and two children in the village of Yuracyacu.

There were reports that about 100 people were missing in the isolated area, local government official for the San Martin department, Hector Valuerde, told radio station Radioprogramas del Peru on Thursday.
Fujimori was expected to fly to the affected villages later on Thursday.
